newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senators demand action against Canada wheat.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senators demand action against Canada wheat.

text.p: North Dakota's senators on Wednesday demanded "immediate U.S. action" to stop Canada from exceeding the voluntary wheat export limits agreed upon two years ago.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky were scheduled to hold a private meeting at 1730 EDT/2130 GMT with Sens. Byron Dorgan and Kent Conrad.

"New figures have come out that indicate Canada has no intention of abiding by the limits it agreed to in 1994. When you're presented with that kind of evidence, something has to be done," said a spokesman for Dorgan.
The two senators, both Democrats, will ask Barshefsky to cut off any further wheat or durum shipments from Canada this year, he said.

A second option is for USDA to activate its dormant Export Enhancement Program to subsidize U.S. wheat producers and help them go after increased market share in countries where Canada is selling a lot of wheat and durum, the spokesman said.
In 1994, Canada agreed to voluntarily limit its annual exports to the U.S. to 11 million bushels of durum and 38.6 million bushels of wheat.

But the North Dakota Wheat Commission, a state agency, recently gathered data indicating that Canada had exported 12.4 million bushels of durum and 50.2 million bushels of wheat during the marketing year that ended in May 1997.
"These figures aren't even close to the voluntary targets that they agreed to," the spokesman said. "They have blatantly disregarded the agreement and flooded our markets."

The Canadian government's voluntary 1.5 million tonne limit on wheat exports expired after the 1994/95 crop year, and Canada has maintained that current grain exports simply reflect strong U.S. demand.

The Clinton Administration told Canada earlier this year it would act if wheat exports exceeded more than 1.5 million tonnes a year. Canada responded at the time that it doubted exports would exceed that level.
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman has repeatedly said he is monitoring Canadian wheat exports closely and would not tolerate market disruptions.

Earlier this month, Glickman confirmed that USDA was considering renewing export subsidies for wheat flour and barley malt, but that market conditions did not yet justify reactivating subsidies for wheat and other bulk commodities.
